# Modelling cellular interactions {#sec-communities}

Microbes rarely live alone. In the gut, the soil and the ocean, they live in communities, where one organism's waste is another's food, and many species cannot be grown in the laboratory at all without their partners. Constraint-based models extend naturally to such communities: each organism keeps its own metabolic network, and the networks are coupled through the metabolites they take up from and release into a shared environment. In this chapter, we build a community model of two *E. coli* mutants that can grow only together. We also look at two other ways of modelling communities: association networks, inferred from the co-occurrence of microbes, and the generalised Lotka–Volterra model of interacting populations. Finally, we turn to infections, with a classic model of viral dynamics within a host.

## Microbial communities

### Network-based approaches

Microbial association networks are inferred from the co-occurrence of taxa across many samples. There is a serious pitfall, however: sequencing measures *relative* abundances, which must add up to one. If one taxon blooms, all the others must fall, as fractions of the whole, even if their numbers do not change at all. To see how much this matters, we simulate 10 taxa whose absolute abundances vary entirely independently across 200 samples, one of them dominant, and look for associations in three ways: in the absolute abundances, in the relative abundances, and after the centred log-ratio (CLR) transformation used by methods such as SparCC.

The absolute abundances show essentially no associations, as they should (one "edge", by chance). The relative abundances show 11, and every taxon appears to be negatively associated with the dominant one ($r = -0.42$, on average), although none of them is. The CLR transformation removes most of this artefact (3 edges), but leaves a small negative bias in every correlation, close to $-1/(D-1) \approx -0.11$ for $D = 10$ taxa. Compositionality is one reason why association networks inferred from relative abundances must be interpreted with great care [@friedman2012].

### Population-based and agent-based approaches

The generalised Lotka–Volterra (gLV) model extends the predator–prey model of §1.5.1 to any number of species, $\dot{x}_i = x_i\left(r_i + \sum_j a_{ij}x_j\right)$. Here, $r_i$ is the growth rate of species $i$ on its own, $a_{ii} < 0$ limits its growth, and $a_{ij}$ captures the effect of species $j$ on species $i$: negative for competition, positive for, say, cross-feeding. We simulate a community of three species, find the steady state at which all three coexist, and check its stability. Then, as one must with real data, we turn the problem around: from noisy time courses of three experiments, we estimate $r$ and $A$ by linear regression, since $\mathrm{d}\ln x_i/\mathrm{d}t$ is linear in the parameters [@stein2013].

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

All three species coexist at a stable steady state (all eigenvalues of the Jacobian are negative). The regression recovers the growth rates to within 6%, and every interaction with the correct sign, but some interactions are noticeably off: species A is estimated to compete more strongly with B ($-0.59$, against $-0.40$), and to benefit more from C ($+0.52$, against $+0.30$). The finite differences used to estimate $\mathrm{d}\ln x/\mathrm{d}t$ amplify the measurement noise, and with only three experiments, some combinations of parameters are poorly determined. Approaches such as MDSINE address these problems with regularisation and Bayesian inference; the fitted model nevertheless reproduces the data well (figure).

### Constraint-based approaches

Strain A lacks both routes to glutamate (glutamate dehydrogenase, GLUDy, and glutamate synthase, GLUSy). Strain B lacks both anaplerotic routes that replenish the TCA cycle (PEP carboxylase, PPC, and the glyoxylate shunt, through isocitrate lyase, ICL), so it cannot make the oxaloacetate and 2-oxoglutarate it needs for biosynthesis. On glucose alone, FBA predicts that neither grows. Such pairs of auxotrophs, which rescue each other by cross-feeding, are a standard way to build synthetic communities in the laboratory [@mee2014].

Community models must decide how the organisms' growth is coupled. Here we follow the idea behind community FBA and SteadyCom [@chan2017] (book, §11.1.3.2 and §11.1.3.6): in a community that persists, every member must grow at the same rate $\mu$, or the faster one would take over. Fix the fraction $x$ of strain A in the community, and express all fluxes per gram of the whole community. Strain A then makes biomass at rate $x\mu$ and strain B at $(1-x)\mu$, and each strain's flux bounds scale with its abundance. For fixed $x$, maximising $\mu$ is a single linear programme over the fluxes $\mathbf{u}_A$ and $\mathbf{u}_B$ of both strains:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\max_{\mathbf{u}_A,\, \mathbf{u}_B,\, \mu} \quad & \mu \\
\text{subject to} \quad & \mathbf{S}\mathbf{u}_A = \mathbf{0}, \quad \mathbf{S}\mathbf{u}_B = \mathbf{0}, \\
& u_{A,\text{biomass}} = x\mu, \quad u_{B,\text{biomass}} = (1-x)\mu, \\
& x\,\mathbf{lb}_A \le \mathbf{u}_A \le x\,\mathbf{ub}_A, \quad (1-x)\,\mathbf{lb}_B \le \mathbf{u}_B \le (1-x)\,\mathbf{ub}_B, \\
& u_{A,j} + u_{B,j} \ge 0 \quad \text{for every metabolite } j \text{ the medium does not supply.}
\end{aligned}
$$

The last constraint couples the strains: a metabolite that the medium does not supply can be taken up by one strain only if the other secretes it. Each strain can exchange at most 10 mmol/gDW/h of each organic metabolite, which keeps the exchanges realistic. We scan $x$ from 0.01 to 0.99, and then, for a 1:1 community, find the smallest total exchange between the strains that still allows the maximum growth rate, to see which metabolites must change hands.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}


![](/examples/communities/cross_feeding/out/python/fig-cross-feeding.png)

Together, the two strains grow, and over a wide range of compositions almost as fast as the wild type: at exactly the wild-type rate, 0.874 per hour, for fractions of strain A from 0.43 to 0.62, and within 2% of it from about 0.14 to 0.69. Outside this range, growth falls steeply, because the rarer strain cannot supply enough of what its partner needs. The model thus predicts which compositions a stable community can have, and that it tolerates a fair imbalance between its members.

The least cross-feeding needed at a 1:1 ratio is simple to interpret. Strain A, which has a complete TCA cycle and anaplerosis, secretes 2-oxoglutarate; strain B takes it up, converts some of it to glutamate with the glutamate dehydrogenase it still has, and passes glutamate back to strain A. Strain B also passes D-lactate to strain A, sharing carbon and energy. Other, equally good, exchanges exist, which is why the automated checks compare only the total. The 2-oxoglutarate–glutamate exchange is the heart of the mutualism: allowing only these two metabolites to pass between the strains still gives 88% of the maximum growth rate.

That the pair can grow as fast as the wild type is a reminder of what the model leaves out. Exchanging metabolites costs nothing here, whereas real cells pay to export and import them, and they release only some of what their partners could use. Real cross-feeding communities usually grow more slowly than a prototrophic strain, and how fast depends on which metabolites are exchanged [@mee2014]. Adding such costs, or limits on secretion measured in experiments, is the way to make the model quantitative.

### Dynamic models

The simplest ODE model of an infection within a host is the target-cell-limited model, described in Perelson's reviews: virus $V$ infects target cells $T$, at a rate $\beta TV$; infected cells $I$ produce virus at a rate $p$ and die at a rate $\delta$; and free virus is cleared at a rate $c$. We use the parameters estimated by Baccam et al. for influenza A infection in people [@baccam2006], and ask how much it matters *when* an antiviral is started.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## Python

*Needs SciPy.*

```{.python include="/examples/communities/viral_dynamics/viral_dynamics.py"}
```

![](/examples/communities/viral_dynamics/out/python/fig-viral-dynamics.png){width=65%}
:::

The basic reproductive number is $R_0 = \beta pT_0/(c\delta) = 10.8$: early on, each infected cell leads to the infection of about 11 more. Untreated, the virus peaks on day 2.3, by which time almost every target cell has been infected. An antiviral that blocks 98% of virus production, started on day 1, stops the infection in its tracks: 99.8% of the target cells are spared. Started on day 2, it spares only 5%, and started on day 3, after the peak, none at all, although it still shortens the shedding a little. Note also that, in this model, the infection ends because target cells run out, and not because of an immune response; models of the immune system (§11.2.2.2) add exactly that.

## Exercises {.unnumbered}

1. Remove the limit of 10 mmol/gDW/h on the exchange of each organic metabolite. How does the range of compositions that support near-maximal growth change, and why? Look at the exchange fluxes for extreme compositions.
2. Instead of fixing $x$, find the largest $\mu$ for which *some* composition is feasible (book, Eq. 11.3), by bisection on $\mu$: for each trial value, solve a linear feasibility problem with $x$ (in the form of the abundance-scaled bounds) as a variable. This is the SteadyCom algorithm [@chan2017].
3. Replace strain B by a strain that cannot take up glucose (GLCpts deleted). Can the community grow? What does the glucose consumer feed its partner, and does oxygen limitation (@sec-extending-cbm) change the answer?
4. Combine this model with dynamic FBA: start from equal amounts of the two strains in 20 mM glucose and follow the biomass of each, allowing them to grow at different rates. Does the community approach a stable composition?
5. Book Exercise 11.2: two genome-scale models are combined into a compartmentalised community model. Work out how many reactions, metabolites and exchange reactions the community model has. How many does our two-strain model have, counted the same way?

## Going further {.unnumbered}

The first constraint-based model of a community, of a sulphate-reducing bacterium and a methanogen, was built by @stolyar2007; it maximised a weighted sum of the two biomass fluxes (book, §11.1.3.1). Since then, many methods have been developed, which differ in how they couple the members: by a common growth rate, as here, by optimising the community and its members at different levels, or dynamically, by extending dynamic FBA. Models of hundreds of gut microbes, and of microbes interacting with their hosts, are now used to study the microbiome (book, Chapter 11).
